rv.q: "Kramer/Fauci" is the most beautiful show I’ve seen this year.

Daniel Fish’s brief, potent Kramer/Fauci makes the argument that in such a moment, this highly transient art form might, in a kind of heroic paradox, come to the rescue, reopening our eyes to what’s been in front of them for decades if we’d only let ourselves look.
How is it so heartbreaking and so hopeful?
Kramer/Fauci is a gripping document that captures something essential about a unique friendship that helped to alter the course of a global disaster.
Kramer/Fauci is high-risk theater-making that pays off as it amplifies a pivotal, passionate conversation of the past.
On the other hand, a neatly resonant encounter has compellingly taken place.
It’s a potent piece of theatre, and, in the final words of the C-SPAN moderator, “an interesting and informative hour” that’s highly worth seeing.
Kramer/Fauci, at St. Ann's Warehouse, turns out to be a bracing staging of a notable hour of broadcast history.
The result is an unusual hour with real staying power, and an AIDS-era odd couple worth spending time with.

Director Daniel Fish, whose dark version of Rodgers and Hammerstein’s “Oklahoma!” similarly featured some distracting avant-garde touches, nevertheless provides a useful historical perspective with this production.
While the reenactment of the debate might have needed some theatricalization, Fish's devices are only a distraction from the men's cogent arguments.

What sets this theater apart as consistently giving their audience pieces that set the bar so high in making us feel and see in a way that sends shivers down our spines and keeps us on the edge of our seats?
The theatrical impact of this form is on full display in the brilliant “Kramer/Fauci,” conceived and directed by Daniel Fish and now at St. Ann’s Warehouse in Brooklyn.
Verbatim theater has been done brilliantly before—The Laramie Project, Dana H., Fatherland—and Kramer/Fauci, even though only an hour, earns a place in their company.
Fish presents all of this material with a directorial flourish that yields moments of surprising humor, a blend of documentary or verbatim theater with elements of theater of the absurd.
That said, Kramer/Fauci is a gripping production.
But this production fails to fully hold your attention, even for an hour in part because they are talking points not fleshed-out characters.

cn.t: Fish's verbatim staging of the 1993 Kramer-Fauci C-SPAN debate earns strong reviews for its piercing relevance and powerful performances, though some find his avant-garde flourishes (foam, lighting) distracting from the already-compelling material.

vr.q: Great performers, really enjoy this start to finish. Go check it out.
